game-alert-triage.intro: Twenty minutes, a queue of alerts. Prioritise correctly.

challenges.q: Alert 1: unauthenticated RCE attempt against an internet-facing server, request seen. Priority?
challenges.why: Unauthenticated remote code execution on the perimeter is the highest severity class.

challenges.q: Alert 2: a user clicked a link in a phishing email but the page failed to load. Priority?
a: Medium, verify no credentials were entered
challenges.why: No successful compromise, but verify credential entry and educate.

challenges.q: Alert 3: a security header is missing on a marketing site. Priority?
challenges.why: It is a hardening gap, not an active threat.

challenges.q: Alert 4: impossible travel for a privileged account. Priority?
a: High, likely credential compromise, revoke sessions and reset
challenges.why: Impossible travel on a privileged account means assume the credential is stolen.

challenges.q: Alert 5: a vulnerability scanner that runs weekly scanned an internal subnet. Priority?
a: Expected activity, close after confirming the schedule
challenges.why: Known, scheduled, expected activity. Verify and close.

challenges.q: Alert 6: an EDR alert shows lsass memory access by a newly installed tool. Priority?
challenges.why: Reading lsass outside known security tooling is credential theft.

challenges.q: Alert 7: ninety gigabytes outbound to a consumer file-sharing domain from a finance workstation at 02:00. Priority?
challenges.why: Volume, destination, data sensitivity and hour all point at exfiltration.

challenges.q: Alert 8: a user installed an unapproved browser extension. Priority?
challenges.why: Policy violation, worth handling, but not an active compromise.

challenges.q: Alert 9: a new domain administrator account was created outside change control. Priority?
challenges.why: New privileged accounts outside process are a classic persistence step.

challenges.q: Alert 10: failed logins for one user from one IP, five attempts, then success. Priority?
a: High, likely brute force success, reset and investigate the session
challenges.why: A small burst followed by success is a successful guess.

game-incident-room.intro: You are the incident commander. Choose the correct next action.

challenges.q: Ransomware is actively encrypting file servers. Choose the immediate next action.
items: Isolate affected segments from the network now
Begin a full disk forensic acquisition of every host
Email all staff to power down
Wait for the encryption to finish to preserve evidence
challenges.why: Containment first: stopping the spread outranks everything else. Acquisition happens after.

challenges.q: You have contained the spread. What comes next?
items: Determine the entry point and check for other compromised systems
Immediately rebuild everything
Notify the press
Delete the malware and declare victory
challenges.why: You cannot eradicate what you do not understand, and attackers rarely use one host only.

challenges.q: You find the entry point was a phishing credential. Which action protects most?
items: Reset the affected credential and all sessions
Delete the phishing email from all mailboxes
Block the sender domain
Warn staff
challenges.why: Revoking credentials and sessions removes the attacker access. The others reduce recurrence but do not remove access.

challenges.q: Legal counsel asks whether notification is required. What do you provide?
items: A factual determination of whether personal data was accessed and affected
Your opinion of the attacker motive
A guess at the number of records
Nothing until the investigation is complete
challenges.why: Notification hinges on data category and whether it was accessed, so that is what counsel needs.

challenges.q: A colleague asks whether to clean or rebuild an affected server. Best practice?
items: Rebuild from a known-good image
Clean the malware and monitor
Restore from the most recent backup onto the same OS
Remove the offending process
challenges.why: You cannot prove a cleaned system is clean, especially with unknown persistence.

challenges.q: During recovery, what should you do first?
items: Increase monitoring specifically for the attacker re-entry patterns
Announce the incident is resolved
Restore all data at once
Disable logging to reduce load
challenges.why: Returning attackers use the same door, so watch for it hard during recovery.

challenges.q: What belongs in the lessons-learned phase?
items: Specific, owned, tracked remediation actions with dates
A narrative of what happened
A list of who to blame
A summary for marketing
challenges.why: Findings without owners and dates do not get fixed, and the incident repeats.

challenges.q: An executive asks for an update before you have scope. What do you say?
items: What is confirmed, what is unknown, and when the next update will be
A confident guess at the scope
Nothing at all
That everything is fine
challenges.why: Accurate uncertainty beats confident speculation, which becomes a quote later.
